lesson.title: Catching Reactions in the Act: Designing Kinetics Experiments
lesson.summary: Because rate laws must be determined experimentally, chemists use controlled methods, most commonly the method of initial rates, to measure how concentration changes affect reaction speed and to pin down the true rate law.
lesson.body:
Since reaction orders cannot be predicted from a balanced equation, every serious kinetics investigation has to begin with careful data collection. This usually means tracking how the concentration of a reactant or product changes over time by monitoring some measurable property connected to that concentration: a color change followed with a spectrophotometer, a pressure change for a reaction producing gas, a shifting pH, or periodic titration of small samples withdrawn from the reaction mixture at set time intervals.

The most common approach for finding a rate law is the method of initial rates. A chemist runs the same reaction several times, changing the starting concentration of one reactant at a time while holding all other concentrations, and the temperature, constant, then measures the initial rate, meaning the rate right at the very start of the reaction, before much product has built up or much reactant has been consumed. Comparing how that initial rate changes as a single concentration is doubled or tripled reveals the order with respect to that reactant, following the same pattern from the concentration and rate relationship: if doubling a concentration leaves the rate unchanged, the reaction is zero order in that reactant; if it doubles the rate, the reaction is first order; if it quadruples the rate, the reaction is second order.

As a concrete example, suppose in one trial [A] is 0.10 M, [B] is 0.10 M, and the measured initial rate is 2.0 times ten to the negative third M per second. In a second trial, [A] is doubled to 0.20 M while [B] is held at 0.10 M, and the rate rises to 8.0 times ten to the negative third M per second, a fourfold increase. Since the rate quadrupled when the concentration of A only doubled, the reaction must be second order with respect to A. Running a third trial that instead varies [B] while holding [A] constant reveals the order with respect to B by the same logic. Once both orders are known, substituting the concentrations and rate from any single trial back into rate = k[A]^m[B]^n solves for the numerical value of the rate constant k.

None of this works without tight control over every variable except the one being tested. Temperature has to be held constant across every trial, since temperature itself changes rate, and mixing that effect in with the concentration effect would make the results impossible to interpret. Precise timing and accurate concentration measurements matter just as much: careless data collection produces a rate law that looks plausible on paper but fails to correctly predict how the reaction behaves under any other conditions, which defeats the entire purpose of running the experiment in the first place.
